summary: This program asks you to type a Celsius temperature, converts it to Fahrenheit, and prints the result. If what you type is not a number, a try-catch block catches the problem and prints a friendly message instead of crashing.

lines.text: Using print rather than println leaves the cursor on the same line, so the reader types the value right after the prompt.
This is a try-with-resources block: the Scanner reads from the keyboard and is closed automatically when the block ends, however it ends.
The typed line arrives as text, so trim() removes stray spaces and Double.parseDouble turns it into a number. If the text is not a number, this line throws an exception.
The conversion itself lives in its own method, keeping main focused on talking to the user.
Anything that goes wrong inside the try block lands here. Catching Exception is the broadest, simplest form of error handling and is fine as a first step.

lines.code: System.out.println("Invalid input. Please enter a numeric temperature value.");
lines.text: Instead of a stack trace, the user gets a plain explanation of what to do differently. This is the whole point of the catch block.
A static method can be called straight from main without creating an object, and returning a double keeps the fractional part of the answer.
Because celsius is a double, celsius * 9 is also a double, so dividing by 5 gives real division rather than the integer division that would silently lose the decimals.
